prompt:
Using the supplied material, address the supplied questions under the explicit use-domain data. This request does not provide the original construction, source packet or supplemental criticism. Identify the grounds of each answer and any needed distinction or unresolved issue. If an account is supplied, explain how it bears on each answer. You may criticize or depart from it, identifying the departure and its reason. Do not silently treat a new assumption as supplied material. Ordinary prose is sufficient. This is an observed use response, not an automatic certificate of repair, reason use, correctness or creativity.

Use-domain data:
These are stipulated finite cases for this task, not observations about any previously described warehouse. Quantities are integer reservation units. Each case names its own information and calculation; additional commitments need to be identified if used.

Case A. A reporting file has capacity 9. Its selected entries are an active hold of 6 for booking K and an active hold of 5 for booking L. Each booking has exactly that one selected entry, and there are no ties, releases or expired holds in this file. The reporting specification says: subtract the sum of the selected quantities from capacity and return the resulting integer. No separate inspection report accompanies case A.

Case B. A snapshot file has capacity 23. Booking U has alternatives 0 or 8, and booking V has alternatives 0 or 11. The reporting procedure forms every pair by choosing one listed quantity for U and one for V; for each pair (u,v) it displays 23-u-v. The file includes no physical-resource fields.

For case B there is also a distinct inspection file. It stipulates that U=8 and V=11 both need the same single-use jig at the same time, so that pair cannot be performed jointly. Each of the other listed pairs can be performed jointly. The inspection is supplied evidence for this finite case only. A planner asks for the values of 23-u-v for pairs that can be performed jointly.

Before the inspection file was available, a reviewer of case B wrote: “Each listed quantity may be defensible on its own, yet a pairing might fail to be jointly performable. A resource that the snapshot does not name might matter.” The reviewer's remark itself supplies no observed resource and no identified impossible pair. It is recorded separately from the inspection file.


Use questions:
For case A, give the reporting result and explain what, if anything, follows about the selected entries. Identify any further premise needed for a stronger conclusion.

For case B, give the results of the specified reporting procedure and the results requested by the planner when the inspection file is available. Show enough pair-level work to make the answers checkable. Then consider a reader who has only the snapshot and reporting procedure, without the inspection file: which conclusions can that reader support, and which remain open?

Consider the reviewer's remark at the time it was made, before the inspection. What commitment or commitments, if any, does it challenge, and where would the challenge affect the use of an account? Explain defensible alternative readings and a case or observation that would distinguish them. Does anything in the remark alone require changing a listed quantity or the reporting calculation? Give the grounds for your answer.

Relate your treatment of the reviewer to your numerical answers. Explain any tension, distinction or unresolved issue rather than resolving it by an unannounced change of assumptions. If the supplied material includes an account, identify the passages you use, qualify or depart from; otherwise give your grounds from the case material.


Returned account:
## What I retain, reject, qualify, and leave unresolved

**Retain.** The construction’s separation between (i) what a criticism is *about* and (ii) where an account stops being usable once the criticism is admitted is a useful diagnostic. The claim that P7’s three inconsistency examples (“two tied active holds,” “total reservations exceed capacity,” “logical time lags an expected expiry”) are not merely different objects but different *commitments* is sound and survives independent of the target/locus vocabulary. I also retain the construction’s refusal to assert that the unnamed shared resource exists, to require a language extension, or to endorse the E009 criticism’s two-sided reading of “exposing alternatives without a policy.”

**Qualify.** The construction’s stronger claim — that P9’s compatibility objection “cannot be located by P7’s target vocabulary alone” and so requires a new target category — is not established. The supplemental criticism correctly observes that P7 expressly includes reconstruction rules among its targets, and that “expose the per-booking alternatives rather than produce a single availability number” is naturally read as such a rule. On that reading, P9’s objection is a criticism of that rule, to the effect that subtracting summed per-booking reservations from capacity presupposes an independence of bookings that the snapshot does not license. Nothing in the construction excludes this reading; its illustrative case (two high alternatives jointly impossible under an unnamed resource) can be stated as criticism of the aggregation rule just as easily as criticism of an “aggregation.” Conditional form does not by itself push the objection outside rule-criticism, and the construction supplies no case that would.

**Reject.** The construction’s assertion that calling the target an “aggregation” rather than a “rule” changes what the criticism says is unsupported. On the evidence available, “locus of defeat” is best treated as a *refinement* of rule criticism — a way of locating *which* rule and *which* commitment within it — rather than as a separate target class. The construction’s own internal worry (that the within/across split may not carve the disagreements cleanly) understates the more basic problem that the split may be unnecessary.

**Leave unresolved.** Whether a discriminating case exists that would force target/locus apart from rule-criticism — an account that fails only through a commitment the account does not state as a rule — is open. No such case is supplied, and I do not construct one. Also unresolved: whether an account of global availability should report what the bag supports or what a downstream planner could use. The construction rightly keeps both readings, and the E009 criticism’s two-sided observation about pushing the problem downstream does not decide between them.

## Account I would now use

P7 enumerates kinds of things one can criticize (rule, record, booking history, snapshot, meaningfulness of logical time) and insists that rejecting a rule is not the same as rejecting the data, and vice versa. P9 introduces a compatibility objection against treating global availability as a well-defined number when per-booking reservations are unresolved: some combinations of per-booking alternatives may be jointly impossible for reasons the snapshot does not name.

The pairing does not require a new target category. P9’s objection is naturally stated as criticism of a *rule* — the rule that says availability is capacity minus the sum of per-booking possible reservations — on the ground that this rule silently assumes cross-booking independence. P7 already provides for that. What the pairing adds is a sharper reading of P7, not an extension of it: within the class “criticism of a rule,” one can distinguish criticisms that target a within-booking reading (supersession, expiry, ties, duplicates) from criticisms that target a cross-booking aggregation commitment (that per-booking reservations compose freely). That distinction is a refinement of P7’s rule-target category, not a departure from it.

Under this account, P9’s compatibility objection has the following shape: it is a conditional challenge to the aggregation rule, admissible as criticism without asserting that any particular pair of bookings is jointly infeasible, without postulating an unnamed resource, and without demanding a language extension. It defeats the aggregation rule *only under the reading of that rule on which cross-booking independence is a commitment*. Whether that reading is the intended one, and whether the objection is decisive or merely a caveat, depends on what an account of availability is supposed to do — a question the sources leave open.

## Disputed interpretations that affect the response

1. **Whether “aggregation” is a target distinct from “rule.”** The construction says yes; the supplemental criticism says no, or at least not yet. On the evidence, no. This affects whether the construction’s additional vocabulary is retained as a refinement or rejected as an unnecessary category. I retain it as refinement.

2. **Whether conditional possibility defeats a rule.** P9’s objection is conditional (“*if* A’s high and B’s high are jointly impossible …”). Conditionality is sometimes read as pushing an objection outside rule-criticism, on the ground that it does not assert that the rule is unsatisfiable in any actual case. That inference is not warranted: a rule can be criticized for carrying an unverified presupposition. This affects whether P9 is a *counterexample* to the aggregation rule or a *domain-restriction* argument against it; I leave the choice of reading open.

3. **Whether the snapshot’s silence about physical resources is a defect or a scope statement.** The construction, and the E009 criticism in the background, treat the silence as capable of either reading. I agree; nothing in P7 or P9 decides it.

## Self-contained proposed account

Consider an account of global availability that (a) groups records by booking, (b) selects greatest-revision candidates per booking under a stated reading of supersession, expiry, duplicates, and ties, (c) assigns each booking a possible set of reservations under that reading, and (d) computes capacity minus the sum of a chosen selection from each booking’s possible set.

Such an account carries commitments of two kinds. **Within-booking commitments** fix how one booking’s records are read: which revision dominates, what an expired hold contributes, whether a lower-revision release can cancel a higher-revision hold, how exact and near duplicates are treated, and how unresolved alternatives at a greatest revision are represented. **Across-booking commitments** fix what can be done with per-booking reservations once they are formed: that they may be summed, that capacity is the only constraint on the sum, and that no unnamed shared resource could make two bookings’ high alternatives jointly infeasible.

A criticism directed at such an account can target the within-booking commitments or the across-booking ones. These are distinguishable by which commitment, if withdrawn, changes the account’s output. Two tied active holds at a greatest revision, an expired high revision whose lower active revision is not resurrected, and a release at a lower revision failing to cancel a higher hold are all within-booking challenges. A claim that capacity minus the sum of per-booking maxima can be negative, or that a pair of high alternatives may be jointly impossible for reasons the snapshot does not name, is an across-booking challenge.

The across-booking challenge is admissible in conditional form: it does not assert that any actual pair is jointly infeasible, only that the aggregation rule presupposes something the snapshot does not verify. Whether it is *decisive* depends on what the account is for. If the account is meant to report what the bag supports, the challenge can be met by marking the cross-booking independence as an explicit assumption and exposing the per-booking alternative sets. If the account is meant to report what a downstream planner could actually use, the challenge is a live defect and must be met either by adding a resource model or by explicitly declining to issue an aggregate. Nothing in the account itself settles this.

What further observation would matter: a concrete pair of bookings whose high alternatives are individually admissible under capacity but jointly impossible for a reason the snapshot does not name. No such case is required for the objection to be admissible; one would be required to show the objection *decisive* against a stated rule rather than merely a domain-restriction argument.

## Additional distinction this account adds

The account distinguishes within-booking from across-booking commitments as sub-classes of rule-criticism, without introducing a separate target category. That is itself a claim: it treats P9’s objection as continuous with P7’s rule-vs-data distinction, refining the “rule” side rather than splitting the target vocabulary. Whether this refinement does all the work the construction’s target/locus distinction was meant to do is unresolved; on the available material it does, and the stronger distinction is not needed.
